passage:
Monday. Rashmi's first month at the new school in Pune, and lunch was still the worst part. She ate on the library steps, pretending to read. That night she downloaded an online strategy game her cousin had mentioned, just to see what it was like.
Saturday. She played for four hours straight. Yash, her friend from her old school in Nagpur, was on it too and kept teaming up with her, typing "nice save!" For the first time in weeks her chest didn't feel tight. When Mummy called her for dinner she said, "Five minutes," and it felt like a hiding place.
The next Thursday. A group project went badly; nobody picked her. She came home, didn't change out of her uniform and logged straight in. It wasn't even that fun anymore, not like the first night. It was just quiet inside the game. That quiet was what she wanted.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi eat lunch at the new school?
qa.a: On the library steps, pretending to read.

qa.q: What did Rashmi want from the game by the next Thursday, if not fun?
qa.a: It gave her quiet and relief from the loneliness and hurt of being left out, which she wanted more than any thrill.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this early stage?
qa.a: An adult like Mummy could notice the long hours and the uniform still on, and gently ask about the new school, so Rashmi has someone besides the game to turn to.

qa.q: What might Yash be experiencing during these games?
qa.a: Yash probably just enjoys playing with an old friend and may not know how lonely Rashmi feels at the new school.

grounding: Shows a lonely teenager at a new school finding that long gaming sessions quiet the loneliness, with relief rather than fun drawing her back.

passage:
Dilnaz, you asked why I get so worried when you go quiet. So let me tell you your Zeenat Khala's story.
When I was sixteen, Abbu lost his job, and our house in Lucknow became all shouting and silences. I felt as if I was holding my breath all day.
One evening on the roof, an older girl from the next building offered me a cigarette. I took it mostly out of curiosity. It tasted awful. But for those few minutes, sitting up there, I wasn't inside the shouting. My shoulders came down.
That was the dangerous part, beta. Not the taste. The relief.
Within a month I was going up to the roof every evening, not because I liked it, but because it was the only place I felt I could breathe. It took me years, and a lot of help, to stop.
So if you ever feel like you're holding your breath, come and tell me first.

qa.q: What happened at home when Zeenat was sixteen?
qa.a: Abbu lost his job, and the house in Lucknow became all shouting and silences.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat call the relief 'the dangerous part'?
qa.a: The cigarette tasted awful, but it eased her stress at home, and that relief is what pulled her back to the roof every evening.

qa.q: What does Zeenat offer Dilnaz, and why does it matter at this stage?
qa.a: She invites Dilnaz to come and talk first whenever things feel too much, so there is a safe person to turn to before a habit becomes the way to cope.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz feel hearing this story from Khala?
qa.a: Dilnaz may be surprised that Khala once struggled like this, and may understand that the worry comes from care rather than suspicion.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager whose first cigarette brought relief from stress at home, and how that relief began a coping habit.

passage:
The school hostel washroom was the only quiet place during exam week. Nazia had come in to splash her face when two seniors offered her a vape. "Relax, it helps with stress."
She hesitated. She'd been lonely since joining in July, and the exams felt huge. She tried it.
It wasn't exciting, exactly. But for a few minutes, her chest loosened and the knot in her stomach went quiet. That was the part she remembered later. The quiet.
Back in her room, her friend Arnab messaged: "Study together tomorrow?" Nazia stared at the screen. She thought about the seniors in the washroom, and about the quiet. She didn't reply for a long time.

qa.q: Where did the seniors offer Nazia a vape?
qa.a: In the school hostel washroom.

qa.q: What did Nazia feel after trying it, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She felt a brief quiet and relief from loneliness and exam stress, and that relief is what could pull her back.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Nazia now?
qa.a: Replying yes to Arnab's revision plan and talking to a trusted adult, like the warden or counsellor, about stress and loneliness.

qa.q: What might Arnab be experiencing when he messages?
qa.a: Arnab likely wants company and support for exams too, unaware Nazia is struggling.

grounding: Shows a lonely, stressed teen trying vaping and noticing that the relief, more than any thrill, is what stays with her.

passage:
Dear Tanvir bhaiya,
I'm telling you because you won't lecture. Last Saturday, at Riya's party, someone passed me a drink with alcohol in it. I didn't really want it. But I've felt so alone since we moved, and everyone was laughing, and I thought, why not.
The weird thing was, it wasn't fun. It just made the lonely feeling go quiet for a while. That's the part that scares me. I keep thinking about how quiet it was.
I haven't told Mummy. Can you come on Sunday? I think I need to talk to someone older about this, properly.
Jaya

qa.q: Where was Jaya offered the drink?
qa.a: At Riya's party.

qa.q: What is Jaya afraid of after the party?
qa.a: Jaya feels frightened that it quieted the loneliness, sensing that the relief could pull Jaya back.

qa.q: What wise step is Jaya already taking?
qa.a: Reaching out to a trusted older cousin, and asking to talk properly on Sunday.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Tanvir would likely feel concerned and protective, and glad Jaya trusted Tanvir enough to tell him.

grounding: Shows a lonely teen trying alcohol at a party, noticing it quieted the loneliness, and reaching out to a trusted older cousin.

passage:
Okay, Kunal, you asked why I'm always online at 3 a.m. Honestly? It started when my parents began fighting every night. The shouting comes through the wall. So I put on my headphones and play. Raids, quests, whatever.
And it works, you know? When I'm in the game, I don't hear anything. I don't feel anything. It's quiet. That's the whole point. It's not even that fun any more. It's just quiet.
Now I play till I fall asleep with the controller in my hand. I'm Jomon, and I think I need the quiet more than I like the game.
You won't tell anyone, right? ...Okay. Maybe the school counsellor. Will you come with me?

qa.q: When did Jomon's late-night gaming start?
qa.a: When Jomon's parents began fighting every night.

qa.q: What does Jomon mean by "I need the quiet more than I like the game"?
qa.a: Jomon feels stressed and overwhelmed at home, and the relief of blocking it out matters more than the fun.

qa.q: What turning point does Jomon reach at the end?
qa.a: Agreeing to see the school counsellor, with Kunal's support, instead of only escaping into the game.

qa.q: What might Kunal be feeling as Jomon explains?
qa.a: Kunal is probably worried and caring, perhaps shocked to learn about the fights at home.

grounding: Shows a teen gaming late at night because it quiets stress at home, recognising that relief, not fun, drives it.

passage:
Monday. In his first week at the new school in Hyderabad, Yash ate lunch alone on the steps behind the library. At home the flat was silent until eight; both his parents worked late. He missed his old friends so much his chest hurt.
Thursday. Karthik from his class said, "Join our squad online tonight." Yash played till midnight, laughing into the headset. For the first time since the move, the knot in his chest loosened. He fell asleep smiling.
The next Sunday. His old friends' group call went on without him; nobody had remembered to add him. Yash put the phone down, opened the game without really thinking, and played for hours. It wasn't about winning. It was about the quiet it brought inside. He noticed, faintly, that he reached for it the moment he felt alone.

qa.q: Who invited Yash to join the online squad?
qa.a: Karthik from his class.

qa.q: What feeling did the game give Yash that first Thursday?
qa.a: Relief: the lonely knot in his chest loosened for the first time since the move.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage?
qa.a: Yash could notice he is using the game to escape loneliness and tell a parent or teacher how lonely the move has been, while building friendships offline too.

qa.q: What might Karthik think is happening?
qa.a: Karthik probably just sees a new classmate enjoying the squad, with no idea the game is covering Yash's loneliness.

grounding: Shows a lonely teen finding that gaming quiets the loneliness, with relief rather than thrill marking the start of a coping habit.
